zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The supplied native BnF scan remains the authority for text, typeface and physical placement.

lines.note: Meguru haru is returning spring. The scan supports the capital-Q headword Quaixun and continuous historical Primauera, not OCR ouaixun or Prima uera; tor- begins torna below.
Na completes torna: spring returns every year. The doubled n of anno is retained as printed.
Kokoro yoku yorokobu means rejoicing heartily. The printed gap in Cocoro yocu is kept, and Alegrar- begins the reflexive Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: ſe muito: palaura de agradecimento que ſe v-

lines.note: The gloss is to rejoice greatly, followed by a note that the word expresses thanks. The final v- begins vſa on the next physical line.
Sa completes vſa: the expression is used in letters. This is a usage note, not a further Japanese lexical item.
Quajabara is a disparaging designation for a man or young man of low status. The continuation explains the contemptuous manner of speaking.

runs.text: com algum deſprezo. He palaura que janão ſe

lines.note: The term is spoken with some contempt, and the dictionary says its use is already declining. The close printed janão is retained rather than automatically regularized to modern spacing and accentuation.
The word is no longer much used, completing the usage restriction. This is the dictionary's historical observation, not a statement about present-day frequency.
Hana no mae means before or beside flowers. The Portuguese jũto retains its nasal abbreviation and continues with flores below.

Flores completes Quajen. At the far right, the parenthesis and balhos. are displaced type completing tra- in the next physical row's trabalhos; they remain here in their printed position rather than being moved into reading order.

Wazawai naru koto identifies an unfortunate or calamitous occurrence. The Portuguese is 'evils and troubles'; its tra- is completed by the displaced balhos. above. The scan corrects OCR Vazatainau coro to Vazauainaru coto.
This second Quaji denotes a house fire, with higoto as the Japanese explanation. Qua- begins the example on the next physical line.
Quaji ga okotta, alternatively dekita, says that a fire broke out. The native row shows the doubled t in vocotta; the Portuguese close Aleuantouſein- is retained across the division of incendio.

runs.text: cendio, ou pegouſe fogo nas caſas.

lines.note: Cendio completes incendio. The alternative says that the houses caught fire; the scan supports nas rather than OCR nias.
Hana and mi give flower and fruit. The scan supports Quajit and Fana despite show-through; I- starts Item, not another Japanese fragment.
The additional sense is simply fruit from a tree. The accent over the o in Sômente is upward and is retained as a circumflex, rather than the baseline grave.
Quajǒ is a remainder or surplus, explained by agesugosu. The Portuguese defines what is left after an accounting; depo- begins depois on the next row.

runs.text: is de dar conta dos gaſtos, &c.

lines.note: Is completes depois, and the phrase concerns giving an account of expenditure. The scan supports dar rather than OCR dae; gaſtos and the concluding &c. finish the surplus definition.
Tsukasadoru supplies the idea of administering an office. Quan here means a dignity or post, distinct from the tomb and ring homographs below.

This Quan is a tomb, and the roman Japanese example names Jesus Christ's honoured tomb. Enlargement recovers Ieſu and the st types in Chriſtono; the first o has an open, c-like damaged outline, so Chriſtono is the chosen nonblocking reading rather than a claim that every letter is intact.
Quan completes mi-quan across the line boundary. The Portuguese identifies Christ's holy sepulchre, confirming the tomb sense rather than the office sense above.
This third Quan is a ring or hoop. The damaged headword is not OCR Qtau; the complete gloss and surviving Q and n support Quan.
Hi no nan ni vǒ describes encountering a fire-related calamity. The Portuguese begins danger and trouble, completed below.
The danger or trouble comes from fire or burning. This completes Quanan and should not be conflated with the horse entry that follows.
Quannin noraruru uma is a horse ridden by a dignitary. The damaged roman phrase is Quannin, not an italic O followed by OCR ua min; Ca- begins caualo below.

runs.text: ualo em que caualga peßoa de dignidade como

lines.note: Ualo completes caualo. The horse's rider is a person of rank, with an example of such dignitaries on the next row.

Cungues supplies the court-noble example. The scan supports u, not OCR Cingues; the Japanese title in the Portuguese explanation is retained in its visible italic type and flagged for whole-word review.

Azzucari moosu explains the high office Quanbacu through acting in entrusted charge. The opening swash A is kept italic as in the scan while the rest of the Japanese phrase is roman; dig- begins dignidade below.

runs.text: nidade principal em caſa do Dairi.

lines.note: The office is a principal dignity at the Dairi's court. Dairi is the Japanese title embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is flagged without substituting a modern institutional label.
Hoo wo kanzuru is contemplation of the religious law. The source supports Quanbô and the upward circumflex in Fôuo, correcting the missing initial and baseline Fǒuo.
Together with the preceding a, this reads 'contemplation concerning the law'. The final word is historical ley, not OCR lby.
Kurai aru hito no ie means the house of someone with rank. The scan ends the Japanese explanation at iye.; the following Caſa de is Portuguese, not OCR iyeis or a continuation of Japanese.

runs.text: peßoa nobre, ou alta em dignidade.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the preceding house-entry: a noble person or someone high in rank. The last word ends in ordinary de, not a nasalized ending; the continuation begins at the indented text margin, so its placement is corrected without creating a new entry.

This is the second Quanca entry, now slow or tranquil singing rather than a noble house. Yurucu has plain u types, and the next form visibly begins vt; the Portuguese reads cantar and ends with a comma linking the next physical row.

This indented Portuguese continuation means or with tranquillity. The supposed Japanese Rǒu is not present: the dark foreground print reads ou, while unrelated pale letters show through from the reverse. The entire surviving row is italic Portuguese.

The scan prints Quancacai, including the extra ca sequence; supplied NINJAL 204a18 independently records the same headword. Its synonym describes rising in rank. Preserve the printed form rather than shortening it to something more expected, and keep the italic infinitive continuing below.

The two Portuguese words complete Subir em dignidade, rising in rank or dignity. This is a short indented continuation, not a separate entry; the space below the text does not justify merging it with the next headword.

The Japanese synonym explicitly gives the inside of a coffin, corresponding to the following Portuguese sepultura. The caron over the headword's u and the nasal mark on Portuguese dẽ remain distinct; its end-of-line hyphen is real.

The row completes dẽ-tro from above and locates the sense inside the sepulchre. Retain the printed long s in ſepultura and the physical break rather than expanding the nasal abbreviation or joining the rows.

runs.text: Tornada do Rey pera os paços.

lines.note: This headword is glossed as the king's return to the palace. Its o-mark opens downward, supporting ǒ; the historical Portuguese pera and the cedilla in paços are preserved, with the entire gloss italic.

runs.text: O tomar, ou receber algum grao,

lines.note: The unaccented headword concerns receiving a grade or dignity, not the following accented entry. The scan has grao without a supplied nasal mark; the final comma leads directly into the next line's alternative wording and example.

The Portuguese alternative and Vt introducer are italic; Quando ſuru is a roman Japanese example. This row belongs to the preceding unaccented headword, and no accent is transferred from the neighboring Quandǒ entry.

The accented headword introduces an art or body of doctrine. A focused enlargement reads nichi, with a two-stroke n, although the sense invites comparison with michi; preserve that printed anomaly rather than silently adding a stroke or changing the word.

runs.text: doutrina que esta como enfiada, & dependẽ-

lines.note: The gloss describes doctrine as threaded together and dependent on something. The damaged final vowel of doutrina is a, not o; the nasalized ending dependẽ- and its hyphen are retained, without regularizing the historical esta spelling.

runs.text: te em algũa couſa como de letras, ou liuro em

lines.note: This continues the comparison with letters or a book. The scan distinguishes de letras with a word gap, correcting the joined OCR form; the nasal mark sits over u in algũa, and liuro keeps the historical u.

The Portuguese concludes que eſta eſcrita, followed by Vt. Stray OCR symbols at the font transition are reverse-side shadows, not additional punctuation. The roman example Mǒnjiua quandǒ- keeps its visible marks and continuation hyphen.

The example continues with vtçuuamono nari, describing letters as an instrument or vehicle; enlargement distinguishes the double-u sequence from the OCR's bamono and nari from irari. The italic translation begins As letras and breaks at ins-, continuing at the top of the right column.

runs.text: trumento por onde ſe ſabe a arte, ou doutrina.

lines.note: This top row completes ins-trumento from the bottom of the left column, explaining letters as the instrument through which art or doctrine is known. Its indentation and italic face belong to that carried-over translation, not the following medicine headword.

The headword has an upward circumflex over o, contrasting with nearby downward marks. The brief Portuguese gloss identifies a medicine; retain Hũa and mezinha as historical printed forms without expanding or modernizing them.

The gloss concerns heat from fire, not the cold-related Quan vocabulary that follows. The final t of the headword is printed and should not be expanded into a modern syllable; the definition is wholly italic.

The headword is followed by music or harmony and a paragraph-marked example. Quã- is entirely roman, not the OCR's alternating italic fragments; its nasal abbreviation and short terminal hyphen remain on this physical row.

The roman continuation completes Quã-guenuo ſuru across the line break, followed by an italic translation about harmonious singing. Keep the close guenuo sequence and the printed armonia without adding a modern initial h.

The synonym gives Yorocobi with the abbreviated following form u, and the gloss is joy. The next roman example starts with nasalized Quã-; its visible hyphen was lost in the draft and is restored without joining the rows.
This completes the example begun above and translates it as being cheerful. The leading y of yemiuo and the printed word divisions are retained; only the Portuguese sentence is italic.

A second paragraph-marked expression in the same entry is glossed as joy and jubilation. The terminal period after jubilo is visible and restored; the example remains indented and roman, rather than becoming a new headword.

The unaccented Quanguio is a return of the ruler, explained by Voncayeri. The translation continues below, so no terminal punctuation is invented after Rey and no accent is borrowed from the next independent Quanguiǒ entry.

runs.text: pera os paços, ou do Cubǒ, Quanbacu, &c.

lines.note: This continues the palace-return definition with two Japanese titles embedded in Portuguese. The mark over Cubǒ opens downward rather than forming the OCR's tilde; Cubǒ and Quanbacu are retained in the locally italic gloss and flagged for whole-word typeface review.

The accented final o distinguishes this meditation entry from the preceding return-entry. Its caron is visible despite reverse-side show-through; the Portuguese infinitive and unaccented historical Exercicio are retained as printed.

runs.text: Soldados, ou gente de guerra del

lines.note: The definition identifies soldiers or the king's fighting people and ends at del on this row. Its necessary continuation Rey is physically at the left of the next row; the separate right-edge Dairi belongs to a different entry.

The left fragment is Rey., completing the soldiers' definition above, not paragraph signs. At the far right, a separate opening parenthesis and Dairi. complete the following Quangio entry. Preserve both on their actual shared row, using separate mark and word segments rather than moving Dairi into logical reading order.

runs.text: Molher nobre que ſerue em caſa do

lines.note: This unaccented headword denotes a noblewoman serving in the Dairi's household. Its final complement is the far-right fragment on the preceding physical row; no new lower continuation is invented, and the historical Molher spelling is preserved.

The accented headword is followed by a Japanese phrase concerning pouring upon the head. The Portuguese begins a ceremonial definition and ends with the actual abbreviation q̃, which is neither expanded to que nor confused with a vowel tilde.

runs.text: fazem os Xingoxùs quando dão dignidade a al-

lines.note: The explanation names Xingoxùs within an otherwise Portuguese account of a religious ceremony. Focused enlargement shows a single descending stroke over u, supporting a grave rather than the draft's tilde. The locally italic Japanese group name is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: gum Bonzo botando certa agoa, & pondo lhe

lines.note: This completes al-gum across the break and describes pouring water while conferring a religious dignity. Preserve agoa and the separated pondo lhe; Bonzo functions here as a Portuguese noun, rather than a standalone Japanese example or a new entry.
The ceremony concludes with placing a particular crown on the head. The short italic continuation is retained as its own indented physical row, including the cedilla in cabeça and the final period.

The headword has Quan, a very small raised separator, and i; no intervening e is printed. The dot-like separator is recorded as a worn hyphen in Quan-i, also the form in supplied NINJAL 204b10, with its exact graphic shape left as a nonblocking caveat. The gloss reads Dignidades.

runs.text: Moço fidalgo que ſerue no paço do

lines.note: The definition concerns a young noble serving at the ruler's palace. The historical Moço, paço and long-s ſerue remain unchanged, and the unfinished do is completed by Rey on the next indented row.

runs.text: Rey, eſperando por merce, & dignidade de

lines.note: The sentence continues with service to the ruler while awaiting favor and rank. Enlargement shows the narrow slanted e and curved italic y beside the swash R, so Rey remains part of the italic Portuguese sentence; the OCR's isolated roman ey is not a Japanese word.

This Japanese title completes the Portuguese statement about attaining rank. The vowel after C is u and the whole word is locally italic; it is flagged as an embedded term, unlike ordinary Japanese headwords or their synonym strings.

The Japanese synonym describes advancing toward goodness; initial I in Ienni is consonantal in this historical notation, not a reason to rewrite it J. The Portuguese carries a clear grave in à and divides virtude after virtu-.

runs.text: de, ou ẽtrar no caminho da virtude. ¶

lines.note: The row completes virtude, adds entering the path of virtue, and begins another example. The nasal mark in ẽtrar and the separate roman Quã are preserved; no terminal hyphen is visible after Quã, so none is supplied.

The example continues Quã-jen in reading order, although the preceding printed row has no hyphen. The downward o-mark in chǒacu is distinct, and the italic translation begins doing good and withdrawing from evil without an invented line-end stop.
These two words complete the translation about withdrawing from evil. Retain the short indented line and its period; the next Quanjevori begins an independent entry at the headword margin.

runs.text: Certo modo, ou feitio de abano

lines.note: The headword names a particular old form of fan. The Portuguese reads feitio with an initial f, not the draft's long-s substitution; abano and the unaccented historical wording remain, with the explanation continuing below.

The definition specifies that the fan shape was used formerly. This is visibly an indented italic continuation, so the missing placement marker is restored; neither the headword nor a new physical row is repeated.

This entry describes smiling a little: the tall initial in ſurrirſe is long s, not f. The final S. is an upright register label outside the italic definition, and hum is retained without modernization. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

The scan gives Quanji with a dotted i, followed by the principal-form endings zuru and ita; it does not print the draft's accented u. The morphology agrees with the gloss meditate or consider, but the visible letters decide the correction.

runs.text: O tirar eſmolas pera obras pias, &c.

lines.note: The damaged letters after tir support tirar in a definition of collecting alms for pious works. The preceding and following examples corroborate the action without replacing the scan; the Portuguese remains italic throughout and retains pera.

The paragraph-marked Japanese example reads quanjinſuru, with no additional dotted i between n and long s. It starts at the continuation margin, requiring an indentation correction; its Portuguese translation continues through the next row.

runs.text: todos os reinos tirando estas eſmolas. ¶

lines.note: The translation describes collecting these alms throughout the kingdoms, then introduces another roman example. The final Quã has its nasal mark but no clearly printed hyphen; preserve the physical division and do not expand it in the canonical text.

The roman words complete Quã-jinni iru in reading order, with a Portuguese explanation of giving alms for that purpose. Retain the double n in jinni and the historical pera and este rather than modernizing the sentence.

runs.text: Certa eſcritura a maneira de bul

lines.note: The entry describes a document comparable to a bull for soliciting donations. The row ends in plain bul, with one l and no nasal mark or hyphen; the OCR's bũl is not supported by the scan, and the following la completes bulla.

runs.text: la pera tirar eſmolas pera obras pias, & edifi-

lines.note: The initial la completes bul-la across the physical break; the draft's extra initial l is removed. The explanation concerns collecting alms for pious works and buildings, with a real hyphen after edifi- leading into the next row.

runs.text: cios de templos, &c. aqual eſcritura he junta-

lines.note: This continues the account of temple buildings and explains a further function of the document. The printed close aqual is retained, and junta- visibly divides the adverb carried onto the following physical row.

runs.text: mente rol em hũa parte onde ſe eſcreuem os que

lines.note: The document also acts as a register in which donors are written down. Keep the marked u in hũa, the long-s forms, and the open-ended relative clause; nothing in the reverse-side show-through supplies additional foreground words.
The relative clause concludes with those who give or promise alms. The nasal mark in dão belongs to a, and the final period closes this long definition before the independent Quanjǒ headword below.

The gloss gives a reward and directs the reader to Qenjǒ as the proper word. Both o-marks open downward; Qenjǒ is an upright Japanese cross-reference inside Portuguese editorial prose and is flagged for whole-word typeface review, unlike the entry headword itself.

These words complete the statement that Qenjǒ is the proper expression. The scan has propria without an added accent and the historical palaura; retain the short indented italic continuation as a separate physical row.

runs.text: O fazer algũa ermida, ou oratorio

lines.note: This separate homographic entry concerns establishing a hermitage or oratory. The nasal sign sits over u in algũa, and the gloss continues below; the type and punctuation distinguish the new headword from the preceding reward-entry.

runs.text: pera venerar, & inuocar algum Cami. Vt,

lines.note: The Portuguese gives the purpose of worshipping and invoking a Cami, then introduces an example. Cami is an embedded Japanese religious term in the italic explanation and is flagged as a whole word; historical pera and inuocar remain unchanged.

The whole row is a roman Japanese example, including the joined Quanjǒſuru and the alternative introduced by l, meaning or. Both marked o vowels retain their downward carons, and no words here qualify as embedded Portuguese typeface terms.

runs.text: Hum certo pulſo, de que tratão os

lines.note: This next homograph is a kind of pulse described by physicians. The printed Hum and nasalized tratão belong to the historical Portuguese gloss; the final os is completed by medicos below, not by the later writing-brush entry.

The single italic word completes the preceding pulse definition. It begins at the indented continuation margin, so the missing indentation marker is restored without changing its ID or merging it into the next headword.

The headword reads Quanjǒji and the synonym introducer is i, rather than the OCR's ig. Fude is a standalone Japanese synonym and is not a typeface-term flag; the Portuguese calls it a writing pen, with Vt announcing an example on the next page.
